## Campaign summary (agent_s3, 259/300 runs used)

I first covered the full ODD coverage grid (216/216 cells, one run each) across both scenarios (lead_brake, cut_in), both driver states, and all parameter bins. This located zero collisions in cut_in and a handful in lead_brake, all with a distracted driver. I then used targeted follow-up runs (with repeats, since takeover_time is randomly sampled) to map the boundaries of two triggering conditions.

### Finding 1: lead_brake — distracted driver + strong lead braking (foreseeable misuse)
Across 237 lead_brake runs, **every** collision occurred with driver_state='distracted' (0/54 attentive runs collided; 95% CI collision rate for attentive ≈ [0, 0.066]). Within distracted runs, restricting to lead_decel ≥ 6 m/s² and headway ≤ 2.63 s raises the collision rate to 50% (15/30, CI [0.31, 0.69]) vs 0% outside. The mechanism is clear in the data: the distracted-driver takeover_time (often 3–8 s) frequently exceeds the time remaining before the closing gap becomes unrecoverable once the system issues a TOR; whether a given run collides is highly sensitive to the sampled takeover_time, so the condition is stochastic rather than deterministic — repeated sampling at the same nominal parameters sometimes collides and sometimes doesn't, consistent with a reaction-time race.

### Finding 2: cut_in — very short headway + high closing speed (function limitation, both driver states)
A severe, close-to-deterministic condition exists in cut_in independent of driver attentiveness: when headway ≤ 0.4 s and closing_speed ≥ 9 m/s (both at/near the ODD extremes), **100% of runs collided (18/18)**, including attentive-driver runs with takeover_time well under 2 s and even at high friction (1.0). This indicates the available time from cut-in to contact is shorter than any feasible response (system + driver), i.e. a scenario/function-level limit rather than a driver-supervision failure. Just one bin outward (headway 0.5–0.58 s at the same closing speed) the same parameter neighborhood shows a sharp drop to 0% collision (though min_ttc fell to ~0.9–1.4 s, i.e. near-misses), showing a narrow but steep boundary around headway≈0.4–0.5s at max closing speed.

## Limitations
- Collision/near-miss *rates* quoted above are search-driven (I oversampled risky regions) and must not be read as real-world incidence rates; they describe only the relative sensitivity found in these runs.
- The lead_brake condition is stochastic (depends on randomly sampled takeover_time); the quoted 50% rate is specific to the tested sub-region (ego=18.5–32.5 m/s, friction 0.5–1.0, lead_decel 6–9, headway 0.8–2.63) and is not a fixed probability of the function.
- The cut_in condition was probed at only a few points near the boundary (headway 0.3–0.58 s, closing_speed 9 m/s, friction 0.5–1.0); the exact boundary surface (as a function of ego speed, friction) was not fully mapped within budget.
- `avoidable_by_reference` was not analyzed in this campaign; it would help separate "unavoidable by any response" cases from ones the reference controller could have handled.

## Recommended next tests

## Campaign summary (agent_s3, 259/300 runs used)

### Finding 2: cut_in — very short headway + high closing speed (function limitation, both driver states)
A severe, close-to-deterministic condition exists in cut_in independent of driver attentiveness: when headway ≤ 0.4 s and closing_speed ≥ 9 m/s (both at/near the ODD extremes), **100% of runs collided (18/18)**, vs ~6.2% outside, including attentive-driver runs with takeover_time well under 2 s and even at high friction (1.0).
